node.label: Ellen Meiksins Wood
node.date_label: “The Separation of the Economic and the Political in Capitalism” 1981 · The Retreat from Class 1986 · The Pristine Culture of Capitalism 1991 · Democracy Against Capitalism 1995 · The Origin of Capitalism 1999 (expanded 2002) · “Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism” 2001 · Empire of Capital 2003 · Citizens to Lords 2008 · Liberty and Property 2012
node.description: A political theorist and historian, at York University in Toronto from 1967, who became the principal exponent of what Guy Bois, criticising Robert Brenner, had called 'political Marxism'. By the accounts of Alex Callinicos (1990) and Brenner (2016), she accepted the label while rejecting Bois's charge of voluntarism. 'The Separation of the Economic and the Political in Capitalism' (1981; revised for Democracy Against Capitalism, 1995) argued against G. A. Cohen's technological determinism that Marxism must not perpetuate 'the rigid conceptual separation of the "economic" and the "political"', since capitalism alone draws that line. The Pristine Culture of Capitalism (1991) turned the Nairn–Anderson theses of a backward Britain around: 'Britain - or rather England - was the world's first capitalist society', and the Continental 'modern' state signalled 'the continuing strength of pre-capitalist social property relations'. She sided there with E. P. Thompson's 'persuasive charge' against an idealised model of bourgeois revolution. In 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001) she traced a line from Marx's 'so-called primitive accumulation' through the transition debate, in which Dobb and Hilton 'challenged the commercialization model', to Brenner, who explained 'the emergence of what he calls "market dependence"'. The Origin of Capitalism (1999; expanded 2002) is unread here: its jacket says it challenges accounts that make capitalism's emergence 'seem natural and inevitable', and McAuley (2001) quotes it on 'the naturalization of capitalism, which denies its specificity' (pp. 7–8). Against anti-Eurocentric histories she held that the confusion of commerce with capitalism was itself Eurocentric. Critics called her position 'little more than a sociology of domination' (Callinicos), faulted 'the Brenner-Wood thesis' for making colonialism marginal (McAuley, after Blaut), and took it to be a caricature of Brenner's (Harman). She answered that slave plantations mattered 'quite a while after the emergence of capitalism in the English countryside'. She also wrote that Christopher Hill's work 'inspired' Brenner's social interpretation of the English Revolution.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Ellen Meiksins Wood (1942–2016); 'The Separation of the Economic and the Political in Capitalism' (New Left Review I/127, 1981); The Retreat from Class (1986; Deutscher Memorial Prize); The Pristine Culture of Capitalism: A Historical Essay on Old Regimes and Modern States (1991); Democracy Against Capitalism: Renewing Historical Materialism (1995); 'Capitalism, Merchants and Bourgeois Revolution: Reflections on the Brenner Debate and its Sequel' (International Review of Social History, 1996); The Origin of Capitalism (1999; A Longer View, 2002); 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (Against the Current, 2001) and replies to critics (2002); 'Christopher Hill and the Recovery of History' (2003); Empire of Capital (2003); Citizens to Lords (2008); Liberty and Property (2012). Readers and critics: Alex Callinicos (1990); Christopher McAuley (2001); Chris Harman (2004); Robert Brenner (2016); Ken Hirschkop (2016).
node.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-18: 'The Separation of the Economic and the Political in Capitalism' (1981), opening sections and notes, in Verso's authorised repost, and the Cambridge Core openings of Democracy Against Capitalism (1995); the publisher's extract from The Pristine Culture of Capitalism (1991), without page numbers; 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001), her two replies (2002) and her essay on Christopher Hill (2003), in full on the Marxists Internet Archive; the abstract of her 1996 essay on the Brenner debate. The Origin of Capitalism is unread; its argument is given through its jacket, her own later summaries and quotations by McAuley (2001). Her acceptance of the label 'political Marxism' is reported by Callinicos (1990), Brenner (2016) and Hirschkop (2016); the passage where she accepted it was not read. She is not presented as the originator of the agrarian thesis, which she credited to Marx and Brenner, nor of the label, which was Bois's. Most of her readers and critics named here are Marxist political theorists rather than historians; her relation to historians runs through Brenner, Thompson and Hill. Her work on ancient and early modern political thought (1978–2012) is listed but not surveyed. The debate she joined is held by the group entry capitalismdebates.

proposed_edges.relationship: Brenner's account of agrarian social-property relations and 'market dependence' as the foundation of her origin of capitalism (1981–2002)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her acknowledgements and uses: 1981 n. * thanks Brenner, and n. 14 cites his NLR essay (Verso repost, read). In 2001 (read): 'Robert Brenner built on the foundation created by these Marxist historians … what he calls "market dependence"'. In 2002 (read): capitalism has '"rules for reproduction" (to use Brenner's term)'. Readers: McAuley (2001), 'she admittedly draws on Robert Brenner's findings and conclusions'; Callinicos (1990), 'Wood's employment of his work to construct "political Marxism"' (p. 112); Brenner (2016) on their friendship from 1978. An exchange between them on the Low Countries (Journal of Agrarian Change, 2001–02) is listed bibliographically and unexamined here.

proposed_edges.relationship: Against Cohen's technological determinism: the 'material base' is social and historical, and the separation of the economic from the political is specific to capitalism (1981)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Verso repost of NLR I/127 (read in part): Cohen's book is used 'to support an argument against a social interpretation of materialism'; 'what Cohen's technological determinism does is to repeat the error of the political economists: he generalizes the particular historical experience of capitalism'. Callinicos (1990, read): this 'is by no means the first time that Wood has used Brenner's work to distinguish her alternative reading of historical materialism from Cohen's' (p. 111). Brenner (2016): 'Here Ellen's main target was … Gerald Cohen'.

proposed_edges.relationship: Thompson's critique of the Nairn–Anderson theses, adopted in her account of English capitalism (1991)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Pristine Culture (1991, publisher extract, read): her preferred thesis 'is more compatible with arguments put forward by E.P. Thompson in the original debate, and less subject to his persuasive charge that Nairn-Anderson operated with an abstractly idealized model of a "Bourgeois Revolution"'. Democracy Against Capitalism ch. 2 (1995, Cambridge Core opening): anyone '(like E.P. Thompson) working somewhere in the fissures … is likely to be badly misunderstood'. 2001 (read): 'Like other Marxist historians such as E.P. Thompson, Brenner understands industrialization …'. Hirschkop (2016): 'The prominence of historians within this group (Edward Thompson and John Saville among others) was probably decisive'. Thompson's 'Peculiarities of the English' is not in the graph and unread here.

proposed_edges.relationship: Anti-Eurocentric histories (Frank's Asian-centred world economy, Blaut's 'protocapitalism') said to share the Eurocentric confusion of commerce with capitalism (2001)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001, read): the critiques 'deny the "superiority" of Europe and emphasize … the dominance, of non-European economies and trading networks' (for example 'Andre Gunder Frank's argument about the Asian-dominated world'). Since Blaut 'does not conceive of capitalism as a specific social form, he can have no clear conception of non- or precapitalist modes of production'. McAuley's reply (2001) and her rejoinders (2002) are recorded on the capitalismdebates → ellen_meiksins_wood critique. Frank's later Asia-centred work is outside the dependency strands, so this is a critique of the tradition's later turn, not of the 1966 hypotheses.

row.context: Against G. A. Cohen's technological determinism: Marxism must not perpetuate 'the rigid conceptual separation of the "economic" and the "political"' (1981; 1995).

A reader of the Historians' Group: she traced Hill's move from an orthodox 'bourgeois revolution' and placed Dobb and Hilton at the start of the line Brenner continued (2001, 2003). Not a member of the British group.
row.works: "Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism" (2001); "Christopher Hill and the Recovery of History" (2003)
